evidence.claim: Its historic setting is the Cape Fear River: Orton Plantation lies beside the river between Wilmington and Southport, and the ruins of Brunswick Town lie south of Orton.
evidence.quote: Located beside the Cape Fear River between Wilmington and Southport

evidence.claim: The town’s historic district contains colonial house ruins, St. Philip’s Church and Fort Anderson.
evidence.quote: The Brunswick Town Historic District contains the ruins of 18th-century commercial and residential colonial homes, St Philip's Church, Fort Anderson, and Russellborough

evidence.claim: Brunswick became a busy port exporting tar, pitch and turpentine for naval and merchant ships.
evidence.quote: became a busy port for exporting longleaf pine products such as tar, pitch, and turpentine used for the Royal Navy and merchant ships.

evidence.claim: British forces burned most of its buildings in 1776.
evidence.quote: The following spring of 1776, a British raiding party from the Royal Navy ship HMS Cruizer attacked Brunswick Town. The raiding party, led by Captain Collett, burned most of the town's structures

evidence.claim: After a few families returned, the port continued functioning, but by 1830 the abandoned town site sold to Orton’s owner for $4.25.
evidence.quote: After the war, two or three families returned to Brunswick. The port was still functioning but by 1830 the town site was completely abandoned and sold to Frederick Jones Hill, owner of Orton Plantation, for $4.25.

evidence.claim: From Orton, the geographic sequence runs south to Brunswick Town, where the church ruins and Fort Anderson occupy the same historic district.
evidence.quote: they founded Brunswick Town one mile (1.6 km) south of Orton.

evidence.claim: Confederate earthworks covered the remains of burned buildings; St. Philip’s Church was left uncovered.
evidence.quote: The Confederates built earthworks and trenches in the town site, covering the remains of several burnt structures except for St. Philip's Church.

evidence.claim: Outdoor trails lead past the excavated fort and town ruins.
evidence.quote: Outdoor trails lead past exhibits and the excavated ruins of the fort and town.

evidence.quote: developed his land into a leading rice plantation with the unpaid labor of hundreds of slaves.

evidence.claim: The house began as a one-and-a-half-story white brick building; a second floor and four fluted Doric columns were added in 1840.
evidence.quote: Originally a 1+1⁄2-story white brick building, a second floor was added to the house in 1840 along with four fluted Doric columns.

evidence.claim: After the Confederate defeat at Fort Fisher, Union soldiers took the property and used the house as a military hospital, sparing it from destruction.
evidence.quote: Following the Confederate defeat at Fort Fisher, Union soldiers confiscated Orton Plantation and used the home as a military hospital, thus sparing it from destruction.

evidence.claim: The gardens and chapel later became a public attraction, but that chapter ended with the plantation’s sale in 2010.
evidence.quote: The Orton Plantation Gardens and family-owned chapel were open to the public until 2010, when the plantation was sold to Louis Moore Bacon

evidence.claim: The plantation and grounds are closed to the general public following the 2010 sale.
evidence.quote: Since the purchase, the plantation and grounds have been closed to the general public.

evidence.claim: Four brick walls survive at St. Philip’s, where fire destroyed the roof, floor, doors and windows.
evidence.quote: The ruins consist of four brick walls

evidence.claim: Construction began in 1754 and finished in 1768, only eight years before British forces burned the church during the Revolutionary War.
evidence.quote: Construction of St. Philip's Church began in 1754, but was not completed until 1768.

evidence.claim: Confederate engineers later built defenses through the town’s ruins, leaving the church uncovered.
evidence.quote: They built earthworks and trenches throughout the town, covering the remains of several burnt structures except for the church.

evidence.claim: Union naval cannonballs struck its walls during the February 1865 attack on Fort Anderson.
evidence.quote: During the attack on Fort Anderson in February 1865, cannonballs shot from Union ships hit the walls of the church and are still evident today.

evidence.claim: The masonry is three feet thick, built with bricks imported from England.
evidence.quote: The bricks used for construction were imported from England and the walls measure three feet (0.91 m) thick.

evidence.claim: Cannonball strikes remain visible on the church walls.
evidence.quote: cannonballs shot from Union ships hit the walls of the church and are still evident today.

evidence.claim: fire destroyed the roof, floor, doors and windows
evidence.quote: The floor and roof were destroyed in the fire, as well as the three doors and eleven windows

evidence.claim: British forces burned the church during the Revolutionary War
evidence.quote: During the American Revolutionary War, British forces attacked Brunswick Town in 1776 and burned the church

evidence.claim: Fort Anderson placed a Confederate river defense over the remains of a colonial port.
evidence.quote: Fort Anderson is a mid-19th-century earthen fort in the lower Cape Fear Region of North Carolina, located over the ruins of the colonial town of Brunswick

evidence.claim: Its earthen batteries supported and shielded cannon, while shelters beneath some earthworks protected troops during bombardment.
evidence.quote: Earthen batteries comprise the fort and were used as platforms and shields for the Confederate cannons.  Beneath some of the earthworks were "bombproofs," shelters used by troops during enemy bombardment.

evidence.claim: The fort was intended to obstruct Union ships and protect Wilmington’s supply route against the blockade.
evidence.quote: The Confederacy decided to build forts around the Cape Fear River to protect the port of Wilmington from the Union blockade.

evidence.claim: Archaeological work later recovered streets and house foundations beneath this military landscape.
evidence.quote: From the excavation, many things were revealed. For example: Brunswick Town's streets and the foundations of houses.

evidence.claim: The visitor center interprets both periods, and outdoor trails pass the excavated ruins of the town and fort.
evidence.quote: The visitor center features displays and an audiovisual program about both the colonial port Brunswick Town and the Civil War period Fort Anderson.  Outdoor trails lead past exhibits and the excavated ruins of the fort and town.

evidence.claim: intended to obstruct Union ships
evidence.quote: The purpose of the fort was to hinder movement of Union ships

evidence.claim: Public garden visits began as a fundraiser after a relative of the Sprunt family was injured in a car accident.
evidence.quote: After a relative was involved in an automobile accident, the Sprunts opened their garden to the public in hopes of raising money for medical expenses.

evidence.claim: Excavations beginning in 1958 recovered bullets, buttons and a cannonball from inside the church ruins.
evidence.quote: Excavations at Brunswick Town began in 1958 and items such as bullets, buttons, and a cannonball were retrieved from inside the ruins.

evidence.claim: Originally called Fort St. Philip after the nearby church, the fort was renamed to honor Colonel George B. Anderson.
evidence.quote: Fort Anderson was built on the ruins of Brunswick Town and was originally named Fort St. Philip, after the ruins of the Revolutionary period church nearby. The name was changed to honor Col. George B. Anderson.
